name: Jam
tagline: Browser extension that captures a bug report with console logs, network requests and a replayable video in one click.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The core trick is not magic: a browser extension can record the tab, hook console and fetch/XHR, grab the DOM and device info, and bundle it all into one artifact. A coding agent will get you a working extension that produces a zip or a local page with video plus logs in a single session. Where it falls apart is the long tail: source-mapped stack traces, reliable cross-browser capture, a hosted shareable link that a teammate can open without installing anything, and the Jira/Linear/GitHub handoff that makes bug reports actually get fixed. If you are a solo dev filing bugs to yourself, the DIY version is genuinely fine. If you are handing reports to other people, you are rebuilding a sharing and integrations product, not a recorder.
coreLoopDIY: A Chrome extension that records the active tab plus console logs, network requests and environment info, then exports a single self-contained bug report you can open locally or drop in a chat.
requirements: Chrome or any Chromium browser for an unpacked extension
Optional: any object storage bucket if you want shareable links instead of local files
whatYouLose: Hosted shareable links that open instantly for anyone, no install, no download
Source maps and symbolized stack traces that point at your actual code
One-click filing into Jira, Linear, GitHub, Slack with the report attached
Cross-browser and mobile capture, plus the edge cases of iframes, CSP and service workers
Team workspace: comments, assignment, search across past reports
moatNotes: The recording is commodity. The value is that the person receiving the bug can open it in one click and that it lands in the tracker they already use.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because bug reporting is a handoff problem, not a capture problem. The moment a second person is involved, you need a URL that works for them with no install, retention so the link still works next week, and a path into the tracker where work actually happens. Jam also quietly handles the ugly parts: redacting sensitive headers, keeping payload sizes sane, surviving single page app routing, decoding minified stacks. A personal build skips all of that because you are both the reporter and the fixer, which is exactly why it works for one person and stops working at three.
notes: Great solo tool, awkward team replacement: the recorder is a weekend, the handoff is the product.
prompt:
Build a Chrome extension (Manifest V3) called "Jar" that captures a one-click bug report from the active tab.

Stack: TypeScript, Vite with the crxjs plugin, plain CSS. No framework, no backend, no accounts, no telemetry.

What it does:
1. Popup with two buttons: Start capture and Stop capture.
2. On start, a content script installs hooks that buffer, in a ring buffer capped at 500 entries each:
   - console.log/warn/error/info calls with timestamps and serialized args
   - window.onerror and unhandledrejection events with stack traces
   - fetch and XMLHttpRequest calls: method, url, status, duration, request and response headers, truncated bodies capped at 32KB
3. Simultaneously record the tab using chrome.tabCapture plus MediaRecorder into a webm blob, video only, cap at 90 seconds.
4. On stop, collect environment info: user agent, viewport, device pixel ratio, page url, timezone, extension version, and the current document.documentElement.outerHTML truncated to 1MB.
5. Bundle everything into a single self-contained HTML file: the webm embedded as a base64 data URL, a video player on the left, and tabs on the right for Console, Network, Errors, Environment, DOM. Network rows expand to show headers and bodies. Clicking a log entry seeks the video to that timestamp.
6. Trigger a download of that HTML file plus a sibling report.json with the raw data.

Redaction: before bundling, strip values of any header or body key matching /authorization|cookie|token|secret|password|api[-_]?key/i and replace with "[redacted]". Make the redaction pattern a constant at the top of one file.

Out of scope, do not build: hosted uploads, share links, auth, source map resolution, issue tracker integrations, Firefox or Safari support, mobile.

Deliver: working unpacked extension in dist/, a README with load-unpacked instructions, and a .env.example that is empty with a comment saying no secrets are needed. Keep it under roughly 800 lines of source. Verify it runs end to end against a test page you create in test/ that logs to console, throws an error, and makes a fetch.
